user.text: Add view transitions to this product gallery app. When navigating from the grid to a product detail page, the product image should smoothly morph between the thumbnail and the large detail image using a shared element transition. Page navigations should slide directionally. Suspense loading states should transition smoothly from skeleton to content. All animations must respect the user's prefers-reduced-motion preference.

history.assistant:
I added view transitions for the product image morph, directional page slides and skeleton-to-content reveals, and turned them all off for users who prefer reduced motion. Type-check, build and a quick server check all pass. I haven't watched the animations play in a browser.

**What I changed:**
- **Image morph:** the grid thumbnail and the detail page's large image share a transition name, so the browser animates one into the other in 400ms with a slight blur. The large image sits outside the loading boundary so it appears in the same render as the navigation, which the morph needs.
- **Directional slides:** grid links are tagged "forward" and the "← Back to products" link is tagged "back". A new wrapper, `app/DirectionalTransition.tsx`, goes around each page's content: forward slides content left, back slides it right. It wraps each page rather than the layout, because the layout stays mounted between pages and would never animate.
- **Loading states:** on both pages the skeleton fades and slides down quickly (150ms), then the real content fades and slides up.
- **Reduced motion:** with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, all view transition animations are off and content swaps instantly. I also stopped the looping skeleton pulse there, since you asked for all animations to respect the setting.
- **Clicks during animations:** the transition overlay lets clicks through, so they aren't lost mid-animation.

The installed `react` is 19.1.0, but Next's bundled React 19.3.0 exports what's needed. No config or dependency changes were required.

**Verification:**
- `npx tsc --noEmit`: exit 0.
- `npx next build`: exit 0. `/` is prerendered as static and `/product/[slug]` renders on demand.
- `next start` with curl: `/` returned 200, `/product/classic-sneakers` showed the new markup, and `/product/nope` returned 404.

**Limits:**
- Using the browser's own back button or swipe gives no directional slide, because those navigations don't carry the forward/back tag. The image morph still plays.
- The home grid doesn't load any data, so its skeleton never actually shows. The reveal there only matters if the grid starts fetching data.
- Browsers without view transition support still work normally, just without animation.

The build also changed some files I didn't touch: it rewrote `tsconfig.json` (reformatted, plus an added `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts` include) and created `next-env.d.ts`, `tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` and `.next/`. They show as untracked because `.gitignore` doesn't cover them. Your existing changes to `package.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md` and `package-lock.json` are unchanged.

3  	description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.

6  	
7  	In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.
8

10 	
11 	React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.
12

export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params

  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<CollectionGridSkeleton />}>
      <ViewTransition
        key={slug}
        name="collection-content"
        share="auto"
        enter="auto"
        default="none"
      >
        <CollectionGrid slug={slug} />
      </ViewTransition>
    </Suspense>
  )
}
```

The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update.

If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states.

## Next steps

You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location.

Each pattern answers a different question for the user:

| Pattern                | What it communicates            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper"      |
| Suspense reveal        | "Data loaded"                   |
| Directional slide      | "Going forward / coming back"   |
| Same-route crossfade   | "Same place, different content" |

For API details and more patterns:

- [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes)
- [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()`
- [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition)
- [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file

    </Suspense>
  )
}
```

The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update.

If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states.

## Next steps

You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location.

Each pattern answers a different question for the user:

| Pattern                | What it communicates            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper"      |
| Suspense reveal        | "Data loaded"                   |
| Directional slide      | "Going forward / coming back"   |
| Same-route crossfade   | "Same place, different content" |

For API details and more patterns:

- [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes)
- [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router), which also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()`
- [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition)
- [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file
